uses.description:
Draws a horizontal divider rule across the text and starts a fresh line, the way a section break is written between two blocks of a description. If there is already text on the current line, drawing first moves down past it, then adds a little extra spacing before the rule is placed at the left margin.

The rule is three pixels tall and, by default, runs across sixty percent of the available width. It is drawn in the standard text palette. The tag itself renders no visible characters.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: How wide the rule should be, in pixels. If omitted or left empty the rule spans sixty percent of the available text width. A value that is not a valid decimal number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Draws a horizontal divider rule across the text in the game's brown rule artwork and starts a fresh line, for a section break on a parchment or wooden background where the standard rule would not read. If there is already text on the current line, drawing first moves down past it, then adds a little extra spacing before the rule is placed at the left margin.

The rule is three pixels tall and, by default, runs across sixty percent of the available width. The tag itself renders no visible characters.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: How wide the rule should be, in pixels. If omitted or left empty the rule spans sixty percent of the available text width. A value that is not a valid decimal number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description: Starts a new line. Drawing moves down by one full line height and back to the left margin, so whatever follows begins on a fresh line. This is the ordinary line break used throughout the game's text, and it renders no visible characters of its own.

Starts a new line with only half the usual vertical spacing. Drawing moves down by half a line height, rounded down to a whole pixel, and back to the left margin, so what follows begins on a fresh line that sits tighter against the one above.

This is the break to use for closely-grouped lines such as a stat block or a list, where a full line break would leave too much air. It renders no visible characters of its own.

Draws an indented horizontal divider rule and starts a fresh line. Unlike the ordinary divider, the rule begins a quarter of the way across the text area rather than at the left margin, giving an inset section break suited to a sub-section or a nested block.

Also unlike the ordinary divider, it does not first move down past any text already on the current line — it only adds a small amount of spacing — so it is meant to be written at the start of a line rather than after text. The rule is three pixels tall and, by default, runs across sixty percent of the available width. The tag itself renders no visible characters.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: How wide the rule should be, in pixels, measured from its indented starting point. If omitted or left empty the rule spans sixty percent of the available text width. A value that is not a valid decimal number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Works out a formula and inserts the resulting number into the text, so a description can state a value that depends on the character it is being shown for rather than a fixed figure. The formula is evaluated against the character the text belongs to, or with no character at all if the text is not tied to one, so it works in both a character sheet and a generic item description.

The result is rounded down to a whole number before being shown. A single space is added after the number, so the tag can be written directly against the word that follows without running into it.

If no formula is supplied the tag inserts nothing.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The formula to work out and display. It is evaluated against the character the text belongs to, and because it is a single argument value it cannot contain an equals sign. If omitted, nothing is inserted.

uses.description:
Works out a formula and inserts the resulting number into the text, but never shows a negative figure — anything below zero is displayed as zero instead. This suits values such as remaining costs, reductions and shortfalls, where a negative number would be meaningless or misleading to the player.

The formula is evaluated against the character the text belongs to, or with no character at all if the text is not tied to one, and the result is rounded down to a whole number before the zero floor is applied. Unlike the plain calculating tag, no trailing space is added after the number.

If no formula is supplied the tag inserts nothing.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The formula to work out and display. It is evaluated against the character the text belongs to, and because it is a single argument value it cannot contain an equals sign. If omitted, nothing is inserted.

uses.description:
Works out a formula and inserts the resulting whole number into the text, rounding down. Negative results are shown as they are, unlike the variant that floors at zero.

The formula is evaluated against the character the text belongs to, or with no character at all if the text is not tied to one, so it works in both a character sheet and a generic item description. Unlike the plain calculating tag, no trailing space is added after the number, so this is the one to reach for when the figure must sit flush against following punctuation.

If no formula is supplied the tag inserts nothing.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The formula to work out and display. It is evaluated against the character the text belongs to, and because it is a single argument value it cannot contain an equals sign. If omitted, nothing is inserted.

uses.description:
Works out a formula and inserts the resulting number into the text without rounding, so fractional values are shown in full. This is the variant to use for rates, multipliers, speeds and percentages, where rounding down to a whole number would throw the figure away.

The formula is evaluated against the character the text belongs to. No trailing space is added after the number.

If no formula is supplied the tag inserts nothing.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The formula to work out and display, shown unrounded. It is evaluated against the character the text belongs to, and because it is a single argument value it cannot contain an equals sign. If omitted, nothing is inserted.

uses.description:
Shifts the drawing position sideways by a given number of pixels, so everything written after the tag is nudged left or right. This is the usual way to hand-tune the spacing in a line — pulling a value away from its label, closing a gap an icon left behind, or lining up columns in a stat block.

The shift is relative to wherever drawing had got to, and it affects both text and pictures drawn afterwards. The tag itself renders no visible characters. If no amount is supplied nothing happens.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: How many pixels to move right; a negative value moves left. If omitted the position is left alone, and a value that is not a valid decimal number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Shifts the drawing position vertically by a given number of pixels, so everything written after the tag is nudged up or down. This is the usual way to hand-tune vertical spacing — tightening the gap between two blocks, dropping a line to clear a picture, or raising a superscript-style note.

The shift is relative to wherever drawing had got to, and it affects both text and pictures drawn afterwards. The tag itself renders no visible characters. If no amount is supplied nothing happens.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: How many pixels to move down; a negative value moves up. If omitted the position is left alone, and a value that is not a valid decimal number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Shifts every picture in the text sideways by a given number of pixels without moving the words. Icons, item sprites, portraits and backdrops all pick up the offset, while the text stays exactly where it was, which lets you correct artwork that sits badly against its label without disturbing the layout of the writing.

The offset applies to pictures placed after the tag and accumulates with any earlier picture offsets. The tag itself renders no visible characters, and if no amount is supplied nothing happens.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: How many pixels to move pictures right; a negative value moves them left. If omitted nothing is changed, and a value that is not a valid decimal number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Shifts every picture in the text vertically by a given number of pixels without moving the words. Icons, item sprites, portraits and backdrops all pick up the offset, while the text stays exactly where it was, which is the usual way to raise or lower artwork so it sits correctly against its baseline.

The offset applies to pictures placed after the tag and accumulates with any earlier picture offsets. The tag itself renders no visible characters, and if no amount is supplied nothing happens.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: How many pixels to move pictures down; a negative value moves them up. If omitted nothing is changed, and a value that is not a valid decimal number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Moves the drawing position to an exact horizontal pixel, measured from the left edge of the text area, so everything written after the tag starts from there. Unlike a relative nudge, this ignores wherever drawing had got to, which makes it the right tool for laying out fixed columns — a label at one position and its value always at another, regardless of how long the label turned out to be.

The tag itself renders no visible characters, and if no position is supplied nothing happens. Note that it does not change where wrapped lines begin, so text that runs on to a second line returns to the usual left margin.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The horizontal position in pixels, measured from the left edge of the text area. If omitted the position is left alone, and a value that is not a valid decimal number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Moves the drawing position to an exact vertical pixel, measured from the top of the text area, so everything written after the tag starts from that height. Unlike a relative nudge, this ignores wherever drawing had got to, which makes it useful for pinning a block to a fixed row no matter how much text came before it.

The tag itself renders no visible characters, and if no position is supplied nothing happens.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The vertical position in pixels, measured from the top of the text area. If omitted the position is left alone, and a value that is not a valid decimal number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Moves the drawing position to an exact horizontal pixel and makes that the left margin for wrapped lines as well, so a block of text that runs on to further lines keeps its indent instead of falling back to the edge of the text area. This is what produces a hanging indent: a bullet or label at the margin followed by a body of text that stays neatly aligned however many lines it takes.

The tag itself renders no visible characters, and if no position is supplied nothing happens.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The horizontal position in pixels, measured from the left edge of the text area, used both as the immediate drawing position and as the left margin for any lines that wrap. If omitted nothing is changed, and a value that is not a valid decimal number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Shifts the drawing position sideways by a given number of pixels and moves the wrapped-line margin by the same amount, so an indent applies to a whole block including any lines it runs on to. Where the plain sideways nudge leaves wrapped lines returning to the edge of the text area, this keeps them aligned with the shifted text.

Because it is relative, several of these accumulate, letting a block be indented one further step at a time. The tag itself renders no visible characters, and if no amount is supplied nothing happens.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: How many pixels to move right; a negative value moves left. The same amount is applied both to the immediate drawing position and to the left margin used by wrapped lines. If omitted nothing is changed, and a value that is not a valid decimal number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Draws a piece of text centred within the width of the text area. The text is measured and the drawing position is shifted right by half the leftover space before it is written, so a short label sits in the middle of the line rather than at the margin.

Unlike the heading tag, this does not add a line break afterwards, so anything written after it continues on the same line beginning at the right-hand end of the centred text. The measurement uses the font the text block started in rather than any font switched to partway through, so centring a line in a different font will be slightly off.

If no text is supplied nothing is drawn and the position is left alone.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The text to draw centred. It is used exactly as written, and because it is a single argument value it cannot contain an equals sign. If omitted, nothing is drawn.

uses.description:
Centres everything drawn so far as a single block, shifting all the text, pictures and timed effects already placed by the same amount. This is applied after the content has been laid out rather than before, so it centres the finished result — which is what you want for a caption, a title card, or any readout whose width is not known until it has been assembled.

By default the block's own measured width is used to work out the shift. A width can be supplied instead when the measurement would be wrong, and the shift can be snapped to a whole number of pixels to avoid the blurring that a half-pixel offset causes on scaled displays.

Anything drawn after this tag is not affected, so it should be written at the end of the content it is meant to centre.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: A step size to snap the shift to, so the block lands on a clean pixel boundary — for example 2 to keep the offset even. If omitted or left empty the shift is used exactly as calculated, which can leave content on a half pixel.

optional.name: Argument 2
optional.description: The width in pixels to treat the block as being, overriding the measured width. Useful when the content includes pictures or trailing space that make the automatic measurement misleading. If omitted or left empty the block's own measured width is used.

uses.description:
Nudges everything drawn so far leftward so that a short number readout appears visually centred, which is how the game keeps a counter looking balanced whether it shows one digit or two. Any spaces in the first piece of text are stripped out first, and if what remains is more than a single character the whole block is pulled left by roughly a quarter of its width.

A single-character readout is left exactly where it is, so the tag is effectively a no-op in that case — which is the point, since one digit is already centred. It should be written after the number it is meant to centre, and it renders no visible characters of its own.

The tag requires that some text has already been placed; using it before any text has been written causes the game to fail.

Right-aligns everything drawn so far, shifting all the text already placed so that it ends at the right edge of the element rather than starting at the left. This is how a numeric readout is made to line up in a column — figures of different lengths all finishing at the same point.

The measured content width is rounded down to an even number of pixels before the shift, which keeps the result on a clean pixel boundary on scaled displays. Only text is moved: pictures such as icons and item sprites stay where they were.

Anything drawn after this tag is not affected, so it should be written at the end of the content it is meant to align.

Adds horizontal padding to the text that grows with the size of the player's screen, and narrows the available text width by the same amount on each side. On a wide display this keeps a block of text from stretching all the way to the edges, holding it to a comfortable reading measure; on a small display no padding is added at all.

When the game is running at an enlarged interface scale a fixed padding is used instead of one based on the screen width. The tag takes no values and renders no visible characters.

Moves the text and its pictures a long way up the screen, but only when the game is running at an enlarged interface scale. At normal scale the tag does nothing at all, so it can be left in place safely; it exists to reposition a block that would otherwise sit too low once the interface has been scaled up.

The tag takes no values and renders no visible characters.

Widens or narrows the area the text is allowed to occupy from this point onward, changing where lines wrap and where centred content is centred. Giving a positive amount lets following lines run further before breaking; a negative amount pulls the right edge in, forcing earlier wrapping — useful for keeping a paragraph clear of a picture placed to its right.

The amount is scaled by the player's tooltip size setting, so the adjustment stays proportionate on larger interface settings rather than being a fixed pixel count on every display. The tag itself renders no visible characters.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: How many pixels to widen the text area by; a negative value narrows it. The figure is multiplied by the player's tooltip scale before being applied, and a value that is not a valid decimal number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Widens or narrows the area the text is allowed to occupy from this point onward, but only when a condition holds. This lets a layout adapt to the situation — reserving room for a picture that only sometimes appears, or letting a paragraph run wider when an optional column is absent.

The condition is a formula evaluated against the character the text belongs to, and must come out greater than zero for the adjustment to happen; otherwise the text area is left exactly as it was. The amount is scaled by the player's tooltip size setting, so it stays proportionate on larger interface settings. The tag itself renders no visible characters.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: How many pixels to widen the text area by when the condition holds; a negative value narrows it. The figure is multiplied by the player's tooltip scale before being applied, and a value that is not a valid decimal number causes an error rather than being ignored.

required.name: Argument 2
required.description: The condition deciding whether the adjustment happens: it is evaluated against the character the text belongs to and must come out greater than zero. Leaving it empty suppresses the adjustment, and because it is a single argument value it cannot contain an equals sign.

uses.description:
Inserts a piece of text into the line only when a condition holds, which is the basic way to make a description say something extra in some circumstances and nothing at all in others — noting a bonus that only applies to certain characters, or a warning that only appears when a requirement is unmet.

The condition is a formula evaluated against the character the text belongs to, rounded down, and must come out greater than zero. When it does not, the tag produces nothing and takes up no space, so the surrounding sentence closes up around it.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The text to insert when the condition holds. It is used exactly as written, and because it is a single argument value it cannot contain an equals sign.

required.name: Argument 2
required.description: The condition deciding whether the text appears: it is evaluated against the character the text belongs to, rounded down, and must come out greater than zero. Because it is a single argument value it cannot contain an equals sign.

uses.description:
Chooses between two pieces of text depending on a condition, inserting one or the other into the line. This is how a description phrases itself differently for different situations — singular against plural, a bonus against a penalty, one faction's name against another's — without needing two separate pieces of text.

The condition is a formula evaluated against the character the text belongs to, rounded down. If it comes out greater than zero the first piece of text is used, otherwise the second is. One of the two is always inserted, so unlike the single-branch variant this tag never simply vanishes.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The text to insert when the condition holds. It is used exactly as written, and because it is a single argument value it cannot contain an equals sign.

required.name: Argument 2
required.description: The text to insert when the condition does not hold. Write an empty value here to insert nothing in that case. It cannot contain an equals sign.

required.name: Argument 3
required.description: The condition choosing between the two: it is evaluated against the character the text belongs to, rounded down, and the first text is used when it comes out greater than zero. Because it is a single argument value it cannot contain an equals sign.

uses.description:
Inserts a piece of text when a condition holds and then stops processing the rest of the text block entirely, so everything written after this tag is discarded. This is how a piece of text cuts itself short — replacing the remainder with a closing note when some condition is met, such as an ability being unavailable or a character being absent.

The condition is a formula evaluated against the character the text belongs to, rounded down, and must come out greater than zero. When it does not, nothing is inserted and the rest of the text is processed as normal, so the cut-off only happens on the branch that fires.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The text to insert before cutting the block short. It is used exactly as written, and because it is a single argument value it cannot contain an equals sign.

required.name: Argument 2
required.description: The condition deciding whether the text appears and the rest of the block is discarded: it is evaluated against the character the text belongs to, rounded down, and must come out greater than zero. Because it is a single argument value it cannot contain an equals sign.

uses.description:
Runs another formatting tag only when a condition holds, which lets any tag at all be made conditional rather than just plain text. Write the name of the tag you want, the condition, and then that tag's own values — for example a picture that only appears for certain characters, or a line break inserted only when an optional section is present.

When the condition passes, the tag is rebuilt from the pieces given and processed exactly as if it had been written directly in the text, including any values that follow the condition. When it fails, nothing at all happens and the tag takes up no space.

The condition is evaluated against the character the text belongs to and is not rounded, so fractional results above zero still count as true. The tag is silently ignored if a condition is not supplied.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The name of the tag to run when the condition holds, written without its angle brackets — for example the name of an icon or line-break tag.

required.name: Argument 2
required.description: The condition deciding whether the inner tag runs: it is evaluated against the character the text belongs to and must come out greater than zero. It is not rounded, so a fractional result above zero still counts. Because it is a single argument value it cannot contain an equals sign.

required.name: Argument 3+
required.description: Any remaining values, passed through in order as the inner tag's own arguments. Write as many as that tag needs, or none at all if it takes none.

uses.description:
Picks one of several alternatives at random and inserts it into the text. The alternatives are written as a single value with forward slashes between them, so a line of flavour text can vary each time it is shown — an idle remark, a rumour, a description of the weather.

A fresh choice is made every time the text is built, so the same line will read differently on repeat viewings. Because the whole list is one value, none of the alternatives can contain an equals sign, and a slash cannot appear inside an alternative.

If no alternatives are supplied the tag inserts nothing.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The alternatives to choose between, separated by forward slashes — for example three options written as one value with two slashes in it. A single value with no slashes is simply always chosen. If omitted, nothing is inserted.

uses.description:
Picks one of several alternatives and inserts it into the text, choosing consistently for a given character over a stretch of about six days of world time. The alternatives are written as a single value with forward slashes between them. Because the choice is tied to who the text is about and to the current week, the same character keeps saying the same thing when spoken to repeatedly, but eventually moves on to something else — which is how a townsperson comes to have an opinion of the week rather than a new one every time you talk to them.

Because the whole list is one value, none of the alternatives can contain an equals sign, and a slash cannot appear inside an alternative. If no alternatives are supplied the tag inserts nothing.

Be aware that this tag reseeds the game's shared source of randomness as a side effect, so other random choices made shortly afterwards will follow from the same seed.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The alternatives to choose between, separated by forward slashes. Which one is picked is fixed by the character the text is about together with the current six-day period, so the same character gives the same answer throughout that stretch. If omitted, nothing is inserted.

uses.description:
Picks one of several alternatives and inserts it into the text, choosing consistently for a given character and never changing. The alternatives are written as a single value with forward slashes between them, and the choice is tied only to who the text is about — so a character's chosen variant is a permanent trait of that individual rather than something that shifts over time.

This is the tag for giving each member of a crowd a fixed characteristic drawn from a set: a favourite drink, a manner of speaking, a home town. Different characters get different answers, but each one's answer never changes.

Because the whole list is one value, none of the alternatives can contain an equals sign, and a slash cannot appear inside an alternative. If no alternatives are supplied the tag inserts nothing. Be aware that this tag reseeds the game's shared source of randomness as a side effect.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The alternatives to choose between, separated by forward slashes. Which one is picked is fixed permanently by the character the text is about. If omitted, nothing is inserted.

uses.description:
Changes the colour of all text drawn after this point, so a word or a phrase can be picked out from the rest of a description — a warning in red, a bonus in green, a keyword in the interface's highlight colour. The change persists until another colour change or the end of the text block.

The colour is named rather than given as numbers, and must be one of the colours the game knows. Writing the tag with no colour, or with an empty value, resets the text to its normal colour, which is the usual way to end a highlighted run. The tag itself renders no visible characters.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The name of the colour to switch to, which must be one of the game's known colour names. If omitted or left empty, the text returns to its normal colour.

uses.description:
Changes the colour of all text drawn after this point, but only when a condition holds, so a value can be highlighted exactly when it matters — a stat shown in red only while it is below its normal level, or a requirement shown in green only once it has been met.

When the condition does not hold, the colour is left completely untouched, so whatever colour was already in effect continues. When it does hold, the colour changes and stays changed until another colour change or the end of the text block.

The colour is named rather than given as numbers, and must be one of the colours the game knows. The tag itself renders no visible characters.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The name of the colour to switch to when the condition holds, which must be one of the game's known colour names. It must be written even if left empty; an empty value resets the text to its normal colour when the condition holds.

required.name: Argument 2
required.description: The condition deciding whether the colour changes: it is evaluated against the character the text belongs to and must come out greater than zero. Leaving it empty suppresses the change, and because it is a single argument value it cannot contain an equals sign.

uses.description:
Inserts the key the player has bound to a particular game command, so instructions and tutorial text always name the key that actually works rather than a hard-coded default. If the player has rebound their controls, the text follows automatically.

The key is shown in a tidied-up, uppercase form suitable for reading in a sentence, and only the first key bound to the command is shown even when several are. If the command has no key bound to it, or the name given does not match any command, nothing is inserted.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The name of the game command whose key should be shown, matched against the names used in the game's control bindings — for example the commands for ending a turn, examining, or using an item. If omitted, nothing is inserted.

uses.description:
Inserts the total time the player has spent in this save, written as hours and minutes in the form "12h 34m". This is the running playtime counter shown on save files and summary screens, not the in-world clock, so it keeps counting regardless of what time of day it is in the game world.

The tag takes no values.

Chooses between two wordings according to the gender of the character the text is about, so a single line of dialog or description reads correctly whoever it is applied to — "he" against "she", "his" against "her", "man" against "woman".

The two wordings are written as a single value with a forward slash between them: the first is used for a male character and the second for a female one. If only one wording is given, it is used for both. Because the whole pair is one value, neither wording can contain an equals sign or a forward slash.

If no wordings are supplied, nothing is inserted. The tag requires that the text is tied to a character; using it in text with no character causes the game to fail.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The male and female wordings, separated by a forward slash — for example a male form followed by a slash followed by a female form. If only one wording is given with no slash, it is used regardless of gender. If omitted, nothing is inserted.

uses.description:
Chooses between two wordings according to the gender of the player's own character, regardless of who the text is about. This is what lets a townsperson's line address the player correctly — "sir" against "madam", "lad" against "lass" — while the surrounding text is attached to the speaker rather than the player.

The two wordings are written as a single value with a forward slash between them: the first is used when the player is male and the second when female. If only one wording is given, it is used for both. Because the whole pair is one value, neither wording can contain an equals sign or a forward slash.

If no wordings are supplied, nothing is inserted.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The male and female wordings, separated by a forward slash — for example a male form followed by a slash followed by a female form. If only one wording is given with no slash, it is used regardless of gender. If omitted, nothing is inserted.

uses.description:
Inserts a character's name into the text. Given the ID of a character in the world, that character's name is used; with no ID, or with one that does not match anyone currently present, the name of the character the text is about is used instead.

That fallback is what makes the tag useful without any value at all: written bare, it names whoever the text is being shown for, which suits reusable dialog and descriptions that must work for any speaker. Nothing is inserted if neither a named character nor a text character can be found.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The ID of a character in the world whose name should be inserted. If omitted, or if no such character is present, the name of the character the text is about is used instead.

uses.description:
Inserts the name of the commodore of the fleet that the text's character belongs to. This is how a hailing message, a ransom demand or a fleet report can name the enemy leader without knowing in advance who is in charge, since the commodore is worked out from the situation rather than written into the text.

A value must be supplied for the tag to do anything, but whatever is written is discarded. The tag requires that the text's character actually belongs to a fleet with a commodore who is present in the world; otherwise the game fails rather than inserting nothing.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: Ignored — the commodore is worked out from the situation and whatever is written here is discarded. A value must still be present for the tag to do anything, so write a placeholder such as a single character.

uses.description:
Inserts the name of one of the player's party members, chosen by their position in the party rather than by name. This lets text refer to "your first crewmate" or the party leader without knowing who that happens to be in a given playthrough.

If the party has no member at the requested position, nothing is inserted, so a tag written for a larger party degrades quietly rather than failing.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: Which party member to name, counting from zero, so 0 is the first. A position beyond the end of the party inserts nothing, but a value that is not a whole number causes an error rather than being ignored. If omitted, nothing is inserted.

uses.description:
Inserts the given name of one of the ships in the player's fleet, chosen by its position in the fleet rather than by name. This is the ship's own name as the player has it — the name painted on the hull — so text can refer to the player's flagship or their second vessel without knowing what it is called.

If the fleet has no ship at the requested position, nothing is inserted, so a tag written for a larger fleet degrades quietly rather than failing.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: Which ship in the fleet to name, counting from zero, so 0 is the first vessel. A position beyond the end of the fleet inserts nothing, but a value that is not a whole number causes an error rather than being ignored. If omitted, nothing is inserted.

uses.description:
Inserts the class of one of the ships in the player's fleet — what kind of vessel it is, such as a sloop or a schooner — chosen by its position in the fleet. This is the type's display name rather than the individual ship's own given name, so text can describe what the player is sailing rather than what they have called it.

If the fleet has no ship at the requested position, nothing is inserted, so a tag written for a larger fleet degrades quietly rather than failing.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: Which ship in the fleet to describe, counting from zero, so 0 is the first vessel. A position beyond the end of the fleet inserts nothing, but a value that is not a whole number causes an error rather than being ignored. If omitted, nothing is inserted.

uses.description:
Inserts the name of the character the player is currently controlling. In a party this is whoever is presently being moved and acted with, which is not necessarily the protagonist, so the name changes as control passes between crew members.

If no controlled character can be found the first party member's name is used instead. The tag takes no values.

Inserts the name of the player's own protagonist — the character created at the start of the game — regardless of which crew member is currently being controlled. This is the tag to use when text should address or refer to the player themselves rather than whoever they happen to be moving at that moment.

The tag takes no values.

Inserts the player's protagonist's name preceded by their current rank title, giving a formal full form such as a title followed by a name. This is what a herald, an officer or a letter would use when addressing the player properly.

The rank title comes from the faction the player currently serves, so it changes as the player rises through the ranks or changes allegiance. If the player has no faction, or holds no rank in it, just the plain name is inserted with no title.

The tag takes no values.

Draws the insignia of the player's current rank in the faction they serve, inline with the text at double size. This is the badge shown beside the player's name and title in the interface, so a letter, a commission or a status readout can carry the same mark.

The icon is placed at the current drawing position and never wraps to a new line, so it is drawn where it falls even if that runs past the right edge. It can be nudged from that position with an offset when it needs to sit inside a frame or beside a name.

Nothing is drawn if the player has no faction or holds no rank in it. The tag renders no visible characters of its own.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: A horizontal offset in pixels from the current drawing position; negative moves left. It only takes effect when a vertical offset is supplied as well, and a value that is not a whole number causes an error rather than being ignored.

optional.name: Argument 2
optional.description: A vertical offset in pixels from the current drawing position; negative moves up. Both offsets must be supplied together for either to apply, and a value that is not a whole number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Inserts the player's current rank title in the faction they serve — the word or phrase that goes before their name on formal occasions. It changes as the player rises through the ranks or changes allegiance.

Nothing is inserted if the player has no faction or holds no rank in it, so the tag can be written unconditionally in text that must also read correctly for an unaffiliated player. The tag takes no values.

Inserts the display name of the faction the player currently serves, so text can refer to the player's allegiance by name without knowing in advance which one it is.

Nothing is inserted if the player serves no faction, so the tag can be written unconditionally in text that must also read correctly for an unaffiliated player. The tag takes no values.

Draws the emblem of the faction the player currently serves, inline with the text at double size. This is the faction's standard mark, so text can display the player's allegiance as a symbol rather than spelling it out.

The icon is drawn at the current drawing position and wraps to a new line if it would not fit in the space remaining. Nothing is drawn if the player serves no faction, or if that faction has no emblem artwork. The tag renders no visible characters of its own.

Inserts the display name of the faction that the character the player is currently speaking to belongs to. This lets a shared piece of dialog name the speaker's own side — "you are trespassing on our waters" written once and used by every faction's guards.

Nothing is inserted if that character belongs to no recognised faction. The tag requires that a conversation is actually in progress; using it outside a conversation causes the game to fail. It takes no values.

Inserts a short description of the fleet the text's character belongs to, of the form used to identify a ship group at a glance — the owning faction in possessive form, whether it is elite, and whether it is a battle or a merchant fleet.

A fleet belonging to no recognised faction is described as neutral. Nothing is inserted if the character does not belong to a fleet at all. The tag takes no values.

Inserts a line of small talk from the fleet the text's character belongs to, describing what that fleet is currently doing. If the fleet is sailing somewhere, the line names the destination and says why they are going: a merchant fleet mentions the goods it means to sell or the investment it intends to make, while a battle fleet says it is going to defend the area, and a fleet bound for its own faction's capital says it is heading home. A fleet with nowhere in particular to be instead asks whether the player is visiting the nearest port.

If the fleet belongs to no recognised faction, or no port can be found nearby, the fleet says it is still charting a course.

This tag can also change the conversation rather than just insert text: if the player is badly out of favour with the fleet's faction, a battle fleet breaks off into an attack and a merchant fleet refuses to talk. It should therefore be used only in a dialog line, never in a description or tooltip. The tag requires that the character actually belongs to a fleet; otherwise the game fails. It takes no values.

Replaces the text with a freshly generated piece of gossip spoken by the character the text is about — a remark about local trade, a rumour about somewhere nearby, or another observation drawn from the current state of the world. This is what townspeople say when they have nothing scripted to tell you.

The remark is chosen consistently for a given character over a stretch of about six days of world time, so speaking to the same person repeatedly gets the same piece of gossip until the world has moved on. It is prefixed with that character's usual manner of speaking, and may itself contain colour and picture tags.

Because the tag rebuilds the whole block of text from scratch, anything written alongside it is discarded. The tag requires that the text is tied to a character, and takes no values.

Inserts the name of a settlement or landmark. Given the ID of a location, that place's name is used. With no ID, or one that does not match a known place, the tag falls back to naming the place the player is currently in; failing that, and only while out on the open sea, it names the nearest place within a short distance.

That chain of fallbacks is what makes the bare tag useful: written with no value it simply names wherever the player is, so a single piece of text can serve every port in the game. Nothing is inserted if none of those can be resolved — for instance out at sea with no landfall nearby.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The ID of the place to name. If omitted, or if no such place exists, the player's current location is named instead, falling back to the nearest place when out on the open sea.

uses.description:
Inserts the name of a settlement or landmark and centres it within the width of the text area, for use as a heading over a port's details. Given the ID of a location that place's name is used; with no ID, or one that does not match a known place, the tag falls back to naming the place the player is currently in, and failing that, while out on the open sea, the nearest place within a short distance.

The name is measured and the drawing position shifted right by half the leftover space before it is written. The measurement uses the font the text block started in rather than any font switched to partway through, so centring a heading in a different font will be slightly off. Nothing is inserted if no place can be resolved.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The ID of the place to name. If omitted, or if no such place exists, the player's current location is named instead, falling back to the nearest place when out on the open sea.

uses.description:
Shows which faction holds the place the player is currently in, as an emblem followed by a short description. The emblem is drawn inline at double size and is followed by wording that depends on the standing: a place wholly given over to one faction is named as that faction's port, or its capital if it is the seat of power, while a place merely leaning one way is described as allied with that faction. A port beholden to nobody is described as neutral.

Nothing is shown at all if the player is not in a place — out at sea, for instance. The tag takes no values.

Shows which faction holds the place the player is currently in, as an emblem followed by a short description, with the description centred within the width of the text area for use as a heading. A place wholly given over to one faction is named as that faction's port, or its capital if it is the seat of power, while a place merely leaning one way is described as allied with that faction. A port beholden to nobody is described as neutral.

The centring allows for the width of the emblem drawn before the text, so the emblem and the wording read as one centred unit. It is measured in the font the text block started in rather than any font switched to partway through. Nothing is shown at all if the player is not in a place — out at sea, for instance.

The tag takes no values.

Inserts a sentence describing how contested the place the player is currently in is, comparing the faction that holds it against its nearest rival. The wording varies with how large the gap is — from two factions closely vying for favour, through a port that merely favours one side while another is not far behind, up to a port heavily favouring its holder. A place given over entirely to one faction is described as ever loyal to it.

This is the readout that tells a player whether there is still room to shift a port's allegiance. Nothing is inserted if the player is not in a place. The tag takes no values.

Draws the emblem of the faction holding the place the player is currently in, inline with the text at double size and with no accompanying wording. A port beholden to nobody shows the neutral mark instead.

Nothing is drawn if the player is not in a place — out at sea, for instance. The tag renders no visible characters of its own and takes no values.

Inserts the display name of the faction holding the place the player is currently in, so text can name the local power without knowing in advance which one it is.

Nothing is inserted if the player is not in a place, or if the place is contested evenly enough that no single faction holds it. The tag takes no values.

Inserts the possessive form of the name of the faction holding the place the player is currently in — the form that reads correctly before a noun, as in a faction's port or a faction's fleet. This lets a sentence attribute something to the local power grammatically.

Nothing is inserted if the player is not in a place, or if the place is contested evenly enough that no single faction holds it. The tag takes no values.

Inserts the name of the trade good that the place the player is currently in specialises in — the commodity it produces and sells cheaply, and the reason a trader would call there.

Nothing is inserted if the player is not in a place, or if that place has no trade speciality. The tag takes no values.

Inserts the base value of the trade good that the place the player is currently in specialises in, as a number. This is the commodity's intrinsic worth rather than the price after the port's own market rate is applied, so it serves as the reference figure a market rate is read against.

Nothing is inserted if the player is not in a place, or if that place has no trade speciality. The tag takes no values.

Draws the sprite of the trade good that the place the player is currently in specialises in, inline with the text at double size, so a port's commodity can be shown as a picture beside its name.

Nothing is drawn if the player is not in a place, or if that place has no trade speciality. The tag renders no visible characters of its own and takes no values.

Inserts the current market rate of the place the player is currently in — the percentage that its prices are running at, which is what makes a port worth selling into or worth avoiding. The figure is rounded up to a whole number.

If the rate is going to change overnight, the coming rate is shown after it separated by a greater-than sign, giving the player advance notice of a rise or fall so they can decide whether to trade now or wait. The projected rate is never shown as lower than twenty. Nothing is inserted if the player is not in a place.

The tag takes no values.

Draws the sprite of the dish served by the eatery in the place the player is currently in, inline with the text at double size. Eating at a port's cafe restores crew morale and grants lasting effects, and this shows what is on the menu.

Nothing is drawn if the player is not in a place, or if that place serves no food. The tag renders no visible characters of its own and takes no values.

Inserts the name of the dish served by the eatery in the place the player is currently in, so a menu or a signpost can name what is on offer without it being written into the text for each port.

Nothing is inserted if the player is not in a place, or if that place serves no food. The tag takes no values.

Inserts the description of the dish served by the eatery in the place the player is currently in — the flavour text that would appear on the item itself, giving a sense of what it is rather than what it does.

Nothing is inserted if the player is not in a place, or if that place serves no food. The tag takes no values.

Lays out the full effects of the dish served by the eatery in the place the player is currently in, as a menu listing rather than a single line. The morale gain is shown first as a percentage beside the morale symbol, and then each lasting effect gets its own line: the effect's icon, its name, the amount it changes by with a sign, and how many days it lasts.

Every entry is placed on its own line starting at the left margin, and icons are drawn at double size, so the tag produces a block of several lines rather than something that sits inside a sentence. Effects whose magnitude is not normally shown to the player list just the name and duration.

Nothing is produced if the player is not in a place, or if that place serves no food. The tag takes no values.

Lays out the full effects of a named food item as a menu listing rather than a single line. The morale gain is shown first as a percentage beside the morale symbol, and then each lasting effect gets its own line: the effect's icon, its name, the amount it changes by with a sign, and how many days it lasts.

Every entry is placed on its own line starting at the left margin, and icons are drawn at their natural size — smaller than the equivalent tag for a port's own menu — so this suits a tooltip or an inventory description of the food itself. Effects whose magnitude is not normally shown to the player list just the name and duration.

If no item is named, the tag falls back to the dish served by the place the player is currently in. Nothing is produced if the item does not exist, or if there is no fallback to be had.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The ID of the food item whose effects should be listed. If omitted, the dish served by the place the player is currently in is used instead; if that does not exist either, nothing is produced.

uses.description:
Inserts a multi-line summary of a character's career: their name and class on the first line, followed by the total experience they have earned, the total damage they have taken, and the number of times they have been knocked out, each on its own line.

This is the block of statistics shown on a character's record. Nothing is inserted if the named character is not present in the world.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The ID of the character in the world whose career summary should be inserted. A name that matches nobody present inserts nothing, but the value must be written or the game fails.

uses.description:
Draws the icons of a character's most-used abilities inline with the text, at double size and in the colours of the class each ability belongs to. Up to five are shown, ordered from most used down, and only abilities the character can currently use are counted — so the row reflects how that character is actually played rather than what they happen to have learnt.

Nothing is drawn if the character has used fewer than two different abilities, which keeps the row from appearing on a character with no history worth showing.

Be careful with this tag: if the named character is not present in the world, it does not merely draw nothing — it wipes out all of the text and pictures placed before it in the block. It should only be used where the character is certain to exist.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The ID of the character in the world whose favourite abilities should be shown. If the name matches nobody present, everything already placed in the text block is discarded, so the value must name a character who is genuinely there.

uses.description:
Inserts the number of journal entries the player has discovered so far, as a whole number. This is the running count used on progress and summary screens to show how much of the game's recorded lore has been uncovered.

The tag takes no values.

Inserts the total number of enemies the player has defeated across the whole game, as a whole number. Every kind of foe is counted together, so this is a lifetime tally for the save rather than a figure for the current battle or region.

The tag takes no values.

Inserts the total number of times members of the player's party have been knocked out, as a running tally for the whole save. Crew currently sailing, crew left ashore at the barracks, crew who have since died, and crew who have gone missing all contribute, so the figure is a complete record rather than a count for the present crew only.

The tag takes no values.

Inserts the number of the player's crew who have died permanently, as a whole number. This counts only those lost for good, not those merely knocked out in battle and recovered afterwards.

The tag takes no values.

Replaces the entire block of text with the contents of a global variable, when that variable holds anything. This lets a piece of text be substituted wholesale at runtime — a sign whose wording is set by an event, a notice board written by the game rather than by the mod, a line rewritten as a quest progresses.

If the variable is empty or holds the single character 0, the text is left as written, so the tag can be placed in a default piece of text that only sometimes gets overridden. Everything that would have been drawn after this tag is abandoned either way, since the block is rebuilt from scratch, so it belongs at the very start of the text.

The replacement text is itself processed for formatting tags, so the variable may hold tags of its own.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The name of the global variable to take the replacement text from. If it is empty or holds the single character 0, no replacement happens and the original text stands. The value must be written or the game fails.

uses.description:
Inserts the contents of a global variable into the text as it stands, which is the plainest way to show a value the game is keeping track of — a name the player chose, a count the game has been keeping, a piece of state set by an earlier event.

The value is inserted exactly as stored, including the literal 0 when the variable holds zero. If no variable is named, nothing is inserted.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The name of the global variable whose contents should be inserted. An unset variable inserts nothing. If omitted, nothing is inserted.

uses.description:
Inserts the contents of a global variable into the text, but treats a stored value of 0 as nothing at all. This suits a variable used as an optional extra — a bonus, a title, a suffix — where the number zero means "there isn't one" rather than being a figure worth showing.

Any other value, including a negative number, is inserted exactly as stored. If no variable is named, nothing is inserted.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The name of the global variable whose contents should be inserted. A variable holding the single character 0 inserts nothing, as does an unset one. If omitted, nothing is inserted.

uses.description:
Inserts a map position written as latitude and longitude, of the form used on charts and in sailing directions — a number of degrees north or south, then a number east or west. Given two numbers, they are read as a position on the world map and converted directly.

This is the form to use when a piece of text needs to quote a fixed spot that is not a settlement: a wreck, a rendezvous, a patch of open water. Nothing is inserted before the game has finished loading, or if the position falls off the western edge of the map.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The east-west position on the world map. Positions right of the map's centre come out as east, left of it as west.

required.name: Argument 2
required.description: The north-south position on the world map. Positions below the map's centre come out as south, above it as north.

uses.description:
Inserts the latitude and longitude of a named settlement or landmark, of the form used on charts and in sailing directions — a number of degrees north or south, then a number east or west. This lets a piece of text give a place's bearings without those numbers being written out, so they follow automatically if the map changes.

Nothing is inserted before the game has finished loading, or if the named place does not exist.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The ID of the place whose bearings should be inserted, which must be a place on the world map. A name that matches nothing inserts nothing.

uses.description:
Inserts the player's current latitude and longitude, of the form used on charts and in sailing directions — a number of degrees north or south, then a number east or west. This is the readout that tells a sailor where they are.

While the player is out on the world map their own position is used. While they are somewhere else — inside a town, a dungeon or a battle — the position of the place they are in is used instead, so the reading still makes sense. Nothing is inserted before the game has finished loading, or if neither can be determined.

Draws a small clock face showing the current time of day in the world, inline with the text at double size. The hand advances through twenty-four positions over the course of a day, so the picture reads as a glance at the sky rather than a precise time.

The icon is never wrapped to a new line, so it is drawn where it falls. The tag renders no visible characters of its own and takes no values.

Inserts the number of the current day in the world, counting from one on the first day of the game. This is the figure used on log entries, contracts and anything else that needs to date itself.

The tag takes no values.

Inserts the current time of day in the world as a clock reading, written as hours and minutes followed by whether it is morning or evening — the twelve-hour form a character would actually speak.

Minutes are always written with two digits, so times read consistently. This is the in-world clock, not the amount of time the player has spent playing. The tag takes no values.

Inserts the name of the current day of the week in the game world. The world has its own named days rather than the real week's, so this is how text refers to when something happens — a market that opens on a particular day, a festival, a shift in someone's routine.

The tag takes no values.

Draws an arrow showing which way the wind is currently blowing, inline with the text. The direction is rounded to the nearest of eight compass points, and a separate mark is shown when there is no wind at all — which is what a sailor needs to know before setting a course.

The arrow wraps to a new line if it would not fit in the space remaining. The tag renders no visible characters of its own and takes no values.

Draws a gauge showing how the crew's spirits stand, inline with the text at double size. The gauge has twenty steps covering the full range of morale, so it reads at a glance as a bar filling or emptying rather than a number.

The icon is never wrapped to a new line, so it is drawn where it falls. When the game's joke mode is switched on the gauge occasionally shows a nonsense reading instead. The tag renders no visible characters of its own and takes no values.

Draws a gauge showing how many days of food the fleet has left, inline with the text at double size. The gauge has ten steps, so a well-stocked hold reads as full and a nearly-empty one as nearly empty — the reading a captain checks before a long crossing.

When the fleet is out of ordinary food the gauge is drawn in an alarming colour, with a different warning shade depending on whether there is a stock of preserved rations to fall back on. The icon is never wrapped to a new line, so it is drawn where it falls. Nothing is drawn if the player has no fleet.

The tag renders no visible characters of its own and takes no values.

Shows the escort contract the player is currently running, as the emblem of the faction that hired them followed by the number of ships being escorted. This is the readout that reminds the player what they have taken on and how large the convoy is.

Nothing is shown once the contract has run past its time limit, so a lapsed escort quietly disappears from the display rather than lingering. The text colour is forced to black for the count, which suits the light background the readout is normally drawn on.

The tag takes no values.

Inserts how many days remain on the player's current escort contract, written in brackets with a trailing d, as in a short parenthetical after the contract's description. This is what tells the player how long they have to deliver their charges.

The figure is rounded down to whole days, and nothing is inserted at all once the time has run out, so an expired contract shows no countdown rather than a zero or a negative number.

The tag takes no values.

Inserts the current value of any named property of a character in the world — their health, their speed, a flag on them, anything the game records about that individual. This is the general-purpose readout used to build character sheets and inspection panels without a separate tag for every statistic.

The property is named exactly as it is written in mod data. If the property does not exist on a character the word "False" is inserted rather than an error, so a misspelling shows up as a wrong value rather than a crash.

Leaving the character blank uses the character the text is about, which is what makes the tag reusable across every character's sheet. Nothing is inserted if the named character is not present in the world.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The ID of the character in the world to read from. Leave this empty to read from the character the text is about, which is the usual way to use the tag.

required.name: Argument 2
required.description: The name of the property to read, spelled exactly as it appears in the character's data. An unrecognised name yields the word "False" rather than an error.

uses.description:
Inserts the current value of any named property of a character type — the definition shared by every character of that kind, rather than one individual. This gives access to a kind's base statistics, its description, its flags and anything else recorded on the type.

The type can be named directly, or a character in the world can be named instead and their type is used, which lets the same text read a type's data whether you have the type's ID or an individual's to hand. Leaving it blank uses the type of the character the text is about.

The property is named exactly as it is written in mod data; an unrecognised name yields the word "False" rather than an error.

required.name: Argument 1

This gives access to a class's colours, its abilities list, its experience track and anything else recorded on it.

The class can be named directly, or a character in the world can be named instead and their class is used. Leaving it blank uses the class of the character the text is about, which suits a reusable class summary panel.
