uses.description:
Lays out a summary of the experience just earned by the player's crew, as a set of grouped rows. Crew who gained the same amount are shown together: their portraits are drawn in a row at double size, and the amount they each gained is written beneath, indented and marked with a plus and the letters xp.

Crew who gained nothing are left out entirely, so the summary only lists those who actually improved. Each group takes its own rows starting at the left margin, so the tag produces a block of several lines rather than something that sits inside a sentence. When there are four groups or fewer an extra blank line is added first, to space out a short summary.

The tag requires that the player has a fleet, and takes no values.

Sets the sound or visual effect played as each piece of the text is revealed during the typing animation, replacing the default click. This lets a piece of dialog have its own voice — a low rumble for a monster, a chime for a spirit, silence for a whisper.

The effect fires once for each piece of text and each picture as it appears, at that item's position. It applies to the whole block regardless of where the tag is written, since the reveal animation runs after the text has been laid out. The tag renders no visible characters of its own; if no effect is named the default is left in place.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The name of the sound or visual effect to play on each reveal step, matched against the game's effects. If omitted the default click is kept.

uses.description:
Reveals the whole block of text immediately, skipping the character-by-character typing animation for everything in it. Text, pictures and queued effects all appear at once.

This is how a piece of text opts out of the typing animation entirely — a readout, a status panel, or a line that should simply be there rather than be typed out. The tag renders no visible characters of its own and takes no values.

Draws a colour swatch showing one of the game's palettes, as a small strip of that palette's colours with a dark backing bar behind it. This is the sample shown in customisation screens where the player is choosing a colour scheme for a sail, a hull or a piece of clothing.

The swatch is drawn at a fixed position offset a long way to the left of the current drawing position, so the tag is meant for a purpose-built layout rather than for dropping into a sentence. It does not advance the drawing position, so several written in a row would all land in the same place.

Naming a palette that does not exist causes the game to fail rather than drawing nothing.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The ID of the palette to show. It must name a palette that exists, otherwise the game fails outright. If omitted, nothing is drawn.

uses.description:
Draws a colour swatch showing one of the game's palettes at double size, as a strip of that palette's colours with a dark backing bar behind it. This is the larger sample used where a colour scheme needs to be seen clearly before being chosen.

The backing bar and the colour strip are placed at different fixed offsets from the current drawing position than the small version uses, and unlike the small version this one does advance the drawing position afterwards, so several swatches written in a row are laid out side by side.

Naming a palette that does not exist causes the game to fail rather than drawing nothing.

optional.name: Argument 1
optional.description: The ID of the palette to show. It must name a palette that exists, otherwise the game fails outright. If omitted, nothing is drawn.

uses.description:
Queues an action to be carried out at a particular point in a line of text, rather than doing anything to the text itself. This is what lets a line of dialog have effects timed to particular words — paying a reward as it is named, playing a sound on a gesture, changing the weather halfway through a sentence.

The first value names which action to perform and the rest are that action's own values; the actions available are listed separately. Written with no action name at all, the tag does nothing.

When exactly the action fires depends on how the text is being displayed. In text that types itself out a character at a time, the action waits until the reveal reaches the position the tag was written at — except for an action written at the very start of the text, which fires immediately. In text that is simply displayed all at once, such as a tooltip or a readout, every action fires as soon as the text is built, so the position it was written at makes no difference.

If the player skips ahead and reveals a typing block all at once, every action still waiting fires together at that moment. The tag renders no visible characters and takes up no space.

Adds an amount to a global variable when the reveal reaches this point in the text, which is how a piece of dialog records that something has happened — a favour done, a secret learned, a count of visits. The change is applied to the game's saved state, so it persists.

The amount is added to whatever the variable already holds, so a negative amount subtracts. A variable that has never been set is treated as starting from zero.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The name of the global variable to change. It does not need to exist beforehand; an unset variable starts from zero.

required.name: Argument 2
required.description: How much to add. Write a negative number to subtract. A value that is not a whole number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Adds an amount to the player's purse when the reveal reaches this point in the text. This is how a piece of dialog actually pays out a reward, settles a debt or charges a fee, rather than merely describing one.

Write a negative amount to take money away. No check is made that the player can afford it, so a charge can push their purse below zero.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: How much money to add; a negative value takes money away. A value that is not a whole number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Plays an animation on the character the player is currently speaking to, when the reveal reaches this point in the text. This is what makes a speaker gesture, flinch, or turn away partway through their own line, timed to the words rather than to the start of the conversation.

A few names are shorthands resolved against the character's own definition — the idle and walking animations, for instance — while any other name is used directly. Nothing happens if there is no character being spoken to.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The name of the animation to play. Shorthand names such as the character's idle or walking animation are resolved against that character's own definition; any other name is used as written.

uses.description:
Adds to one of the player's kinds of renown when the reveal reaches this point in the text — their standing as a fighter, an explorer or a trader. Fame also lifts crew morale a little and can affect what the crown asks of the player, so it is a broader reward than a simple variable change.

Write a negative amount to reduce renown. Fame is never allowed to fall below zero.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: Which kind of renown to change. The game's own kinds are combat, exploration and trade renown; the value names the category rather than a faction.

required.name: Argument 2
required.description: How much renown to add; a negative value reduces it. A value that is not a whole number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Adds to the player's standing with a faction when the reveal reaches this point in the text. This is how a conversation actually makes a friend or an enemy of a power, rather than merely saying so.

Write a negative amount to lose standing. The change is normally announced to the player with a floating number and a sound, so it reads as a consequence of what was just said.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The ID of the faction whose standing should change.

required.name: Argument 2
required.description: How much standing to add; a negative value loses standing. A value that is not a whole number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Pops a floating number or short label above the text at the point the reveal reaches, in the style the game uses for damage and gains in battle. This draws the player's eye to a figure just mentioned, such as a reward or a penalty, and lets it drift away rather than sitting there.

The label appears at the position in the text where the tag was written, so it can be aimed at a particular word.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The text to pop up. It is shown exactly as written, so it can be a number, a signed number or a short word.

uses.description:
Runs a game task when the reveal reaches this point in the text, which is how a conversation makes something happen in the world — changing the weather, opening a gate, spawning something, moving a character. Any task the game supports can be triggered this way.

The task is written in the same form as elsewhere in mod data, with its parameters separated by commas rather than equals signs, since an equals sign cannot appear inside a tag value. The task runs with no position of its own, so tasks that need a target tile are not suitable here.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The task to run, written in the game's usual task form with comma-separated parameters. It cannot contain an equals sign, so tasks whose parameters need one cannot be used here.

uses.description:
Reveals a set number of further pictures when the reveal reaches this point in the text, rather than everything at once. This lets a sequence of images be uncovered a few at a time as the words arrive, for a slideshow or a step-by-step diagram.

Only pictures are affected by the count; the text itself continues to type out at its normal pace.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: How many further pictures to uncover. A value that is not a whole number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Reveals the whole block of text immediately when the reveal reaches this point, skipping the rest of the typing animation. Everything still to come — text, pictures and any effects queued after this point — appears at once.

Written with no count, this is how a line stops typing itself partway through and simply finishes.

Holds the typing animation for a moment when the reveal reaches this point in the text, before the rest of the line continues. This is the same beat that the standalone pause tag inserts, written in command form.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: How long to hold, in the same units as the text reveal timer — larger numbers hold longer. A value that is not a valid decimal number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Plays a visual effect at the point in the text the reveal has reached, when it gets there. Because the effect is anchored to a position in the text rather than to the screen or the world, it can be aimed at a particular word — a flash on a name, sparks on a threat.

The effect is played in its plain white form rather than tinted.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The name of the visual effect to play, matched against the game's effects.

uses.description:
Plays a sound when the reveal reaches this point in the text, which is how a line gets a noise timed to a particular word — a door slamming, a coin dropping, a laugh partway through a sentence.

The sound plays once and does not affect the text itself.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The name of the sound to play, matched against the game's sounds.

uses.description:
Moves the conversation on by itself after a delay, once the reveal reaches this point in the text. This is what makes a line advance without the player pressing anything — a monologue that continues on its own, a cutscene that keeps its own pace, a beat of silence before the next speaker.

The delay is counted from the moment the reveal arrives at the tag, so writing it at the end of a line waits for the line to finish typing first.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: How long to wait before advancing, in seconds. A value that is not a valid decimal number causes an error rather than being ignored.

uses.description:
Opens the player's journal to a particular entry when the reveal reaches this point in the text, with a page-turning sound and, if the player has the fuller visual effects switched on, an animation of the page turning. The journal window is centred and the player cannot interact with it, so it reads as something being shown to them rather than something to browse.

This is how a conversation illustrates itself with a piece of recorded lore — a character producing a chart or a letter as they mention it.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The ID of the journal entry to open to. An entry the player has not yet discovered opens to the end of the journal instead.

uses.description:
Writes a single equals sign. Because a value inside a tag is separated from the next by an equals sign, an equals sign cannot otherwise appear in text without being taken as a separator, and this nameless tag is the way to produce one.

Be aware that this also happens by accident: any stretch of text that begins with an equals sign is replaced by a lone equals sign, and the rest of that stretch is lost. Text meant to start with an equals sign should therefore be written using this tag followed by the remaining words.

Inserts the current value of a global variable as a number, and keeps it up to date. Unlike the ordinary variable readout, which is fixed at the moment the text is built, this one is re-read every frame while the text is on screen, so a figure that changes while the player is looking at it visibly counts up or down. This is what a live readout of money, a countdown, or a running total is written with.

The value is read as a number rather than as text: a variable holding something that is not a number, or one that has never been set, shows as 0. Any spaces in the variable's name are ignored.

Space is reserved for four characters regardless of what the value turns out to be, so a longer figure runs into whatever follows it and a shorter one leaves a gap. Lay out the surrounding text with that fixed width in mind. During the typing animation the value appears all at once rather than being typed out character by character.

This tag is recognised only when written with a variable name after an equals sign; written bare, the letters are simply drawn as ordinary text.

required.name: Argument 1
required.description: The name of the global variable to display. Its contents are read as a number, so a variable holding non-numeric text shows as 0, as does one that has never been set. Spaces in the name are ignored. Anything written after this value is discarded.
